    01

    Child development foundations

    Stages · principles · theorists    +

    Development is patterned, not identical

    Development is continuous, follows broad sequences, moves from general to specific responses and is shaped by heredity and environment. Children vary in pace; difference is not deficiency.

    Three theorists in one glance

    • Piaget: sensorimotor (0–2), pre-operational (2–7), concrete operational (7–11), formal operational (11+). A primary child learns best through concrete material before symbols.
    • Vygotsky: learning is social. The ZPD is what a learner can do with support; scaffolding is gradually withdrawn.
    • Kohlberg: moral reasoning progresses from consequence/self-interest to social approval/law, then principled reasoning.
    Exam lens: choose the option that respects the child’s reasoning and uses errors diagnostically—not punishment, labeling or one-method-for-all teaching.
    02

    Learning, assessment & inclusion

    Constructivism · CWSN · evaluation    +

    Constructivist classroom

    Learners connect new ideas to prior knowledge. The teacher designs inquiry, discussion, peer work and reflection rather than merely transmitting answers.

    • Formative assessment: during learning; feedback changes the next teaching step.
    • Summative assessment: after a unit/term; judges achievement.
    • Diagnostic assessment: identifies the source of a difficulty; remediation follows.
    • Portfolio: evidence of progress over time.

    Inclusive practice

    Keep the learning goal common while varying access: audio/text choice, larger print, tactile material, extra processing time, peer support and multiple ways to respond. Accommodation changes how a learner accesses the task; modification changes what is expected.

    Remember: intelligence is multi-dimensional and developable. A test score is evidence from one setting, not a fixed label.
    03

    Language pedagogy

    Acquisition · literacy · multilingualism    +

    Language grows through meaningful use

    Listening and speaking support reading and writing. Children acquire patterns by using language in context; grammar is best taught through purposeful text, not isolated rule memorisation alone.

    • Before reading: activate prior knowledge, predict from title/pictures.
    • During: question, infer, notice connections, monitor meaning.
    • After: summarise, respond, compare viewpoints.
    • Multilingual class: use home languages as bridges; code-switching can scaffold meaning.
    Skimming = gist · Scanning = specific detail · Inference = meaning not directly stated

    Error treatment: first understand whether the error comes from transfer, overgeneralisation or incomplete rule knowledge; respond without humiliating the learner.

    04

    Mathematics & its pedagogy

    Concepts · formulas · misconceptions    +

    Teach from concrete to abstract

    Use the CPA sequence: Concrete objects → Pictorial models → Abstract symbols. Ask learners to explain strategies; multiple valid methods reveal mathematical thinking.

    • Fraction comparison: use a common denominator or compare distance from 0/1—not the size of denominator alone.
    • Place value: the value of digit 7 in 7,305 is 7,000; its face value remains 7.
    • Error analysis: “1/3 + 1/4 = 2/7” shows adding denominators; use area strips to rebuild the idea.



    Work rate:
    ·
    05

    Environmental Studies

    Themes · inquiry · daily life    +

    EVS integrates science and social life

    Its recurring themes—Family & Friends, Food, Shelter, Water, Travel, and Things We Make and Do—begin with the child’s surroundings and expand outward.

    • Water: evaporation → condensation → precipitation → collection. Conservation works best at source: fix leaks, recharge groundwater, reuse suitable greywater.
    • Food chains: producers capture solar energy; consumers transfer it; decomposers recycle nutrients.
    • Field observation: observe, record, classify, compare, question, then explain. A worksheet alone is not inquiry.
    • Social understanding: avoid stereotypes about work, family roles, gender, caste, language or region.
    Best answer pattern: local experience + hands-on investigation + discussion + reflection.
    06

    Science for Paper II

    Core science · experiments · reasoning    +

    High-yield concept spine

    • Matter: particle spacing and motion explain solid, liquid and gas; heating increases average kinetic energy.
    • Force & motion: net force changes velocity. Friction can hinder motion but also enables walking and gripping.
    • Life: cells are structural/functional units; photosynthesis stores light energy; respiration releases usable energy.
    • Electricity: current requires a closed circuit; series components share current, parallel branches share voltage.

    Science pedagogy

    A fair test changes one variable, controls relevant others and measures the outcome. Let learners predict before observing; a surprising result is an opportunity to revise a model.

    · ·
    07

    Social Science for Paper II

    History · geography · civics    +

    Build arguments from evidence

    • History: sources include inscriptions, coins, texts, objects and oral traditions. A source reflects a context and point of view.
    • Geography: latitude measures north–south position; longitude helps determine local time. Monsoon is a seasonal wind reversal, not simply “heavy rain”.
    • Civics: the Constitution limits state power and protects rights; federalism divides authority across levels.
    • Economics: distinguish need/want, paid/unpaid work, formal/informal sectors and public/private provision.

    Pedagogy: use timelines for change, maps for spatial relationships, role-play for institutions and contrasting sources for critical thinking.

    08

    BPSC TRE: GS & Bihar core

    Bihar facts · arithmetic · reasoning    +

    Bihar anchor points

    • Bihar was separated from Bengal on 22 March 1912; Bihar Day is observed on 22 March.
    • The Champaran Satyagraha (1917) challenged indigo cultivation arrangements and marked Gandhi’s first satyagraha in India.
    • Nalanda and Vikramashila were major centres of learning in ancient/early medieval eastern India.
    • The Ganga flows west to east through the state; the Kosi is noted for shifting channels and flood impact.

    GS solving order

    Start with direct facts, then arithmetic, then multi-step reasoning. In percentage change, always identify the original value as the base.

    Successive change a%, b% = a + b + ab/100
    Population density = population ÷ area
    Distance = speed × time
    Current affairs: this static page does not pretend to stay live. Add a dated monthly notebook from official government releases and revise backward from the exam date.

    TRE language qualifier

    English · Hindi · comprehension    +

    English quick rules

    • Subject–verb agreement follows the true head noun: “The quality of the books is good.”
    • Passive voice: object → subject + suitable form of be + past participle.
    • Reported speech shifts tense when the reporting verb is past, unless the statement remains universally true.
    • Read the question before the passage; answer from the passage, not outside knowledge.

    हिंदी त्वरित पुनरावृत्ति

    • संधि: दो वर्णों के मेल से होने वाला परिवर्तन।
    • समास: दो या अधिक पदों का संक्षिप्त रूप; विग्रह से संबंध स्पष्ट करें।
    • उपसर्ग शब्द के पहले, प्रत्यय शब्द के बाद जुड़ता है।

    1. Child Development: Piaget, Kohlberg, Vygotsky & Erikson

    Erikson — eight psychosocial stages

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    Child development and pedagogy is the highest-weight section of CTET Paper I — and the one where examiners set the trickiest distractors. The four theorists below appear in nearly every sitting. Learn not just the stages, but the contrast points between theorists; CTET loves asking "which theory does this classroom example illustrate?"

    Piaget — cognitive development (constructivist, stage-based)

    Piaget argued children are active constructors of knowledge. Learning happens through schemas (mental models), adjusted by assimilation (fitting new experience into an existing schema — a child calling all four-legged animals "doggie") and accommodation (changing the schema itself — learning some four-legged animals are cats). When the two balance, the child is in equilibrium; disturbance produces disequilibrium, which drives learning.

    The four stages (ages are approximate — examiners test the sequence and hallmarks, not exact cutoffs):

    • Sensorimotor (birth–2 yrs): knowledge through senses and motor action; key milestone is object permanence (~8–12 months) — knowing a hidden object still exists. Circular reactions, deferred imitation.
    • Preoperational (2–7 yrs): language explodes; thinking is symbolic but illogical. Hallmarks: egocentrism (inability to take another's viewpoint — the classic "three-mountain task"), animism (attributing life to objects), centration (focusing on one aspect — taller glass = more juice), failure of conservation, irreversibility, transductive reasoning.
    • Concrete operational (7–11 yrs): logical thought about concrete objects; conservation achieved (number, mass, volume — note the fixed order), classification, seriation, reversibility. Limitation: abstract/hypothetical reasoning is still out of reach.
    • Formal operational (11+ yrs): abstract, hypothetical-deductive reasoning ("what if" thinking), systematic problem-solving, propositional thought.

    Piaget traps: (a) Piaget is a cognitive theorist, not a moral-development one; (b) he emphasised maturation + active discovery — so "child learns best by manipulating objects themselves" is Piaget, not Vygotsky; (c) the moral-judgment work (heteronomous → autonomous morality) is Piaget's too, but CTET tests Kohlberg far more often for moral development.

    Piaget's 4 stages of cognitive development

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    Vygotsky — sociocultural theory (the anti-Piaget)

    Where Piaget saw the lone child-scientist, Vygotsky saw the child-apprentice: cognition develops through social interaction first, then gets internalised ("every function appears twice — interpsychological, then intrapsychological"). Key tools:

    • Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD): the gap between what a child can do alone (actual level) and with guidance (potential level). Teaching must target the ZPD — tasks too easy waste time; tasks beyond the ZPD frustrate.
    • More Knowledgeable Other (MKO) and scaffolding: temporary support (prompts, modelling, hints) that is gradually withdrawn. "A teacher giving hints that she slowly removes" = scaffolding, a favourite CTET stem.
    • Language as the primary psychological tool; private speech (children talking to themselves while solving problems) is not egocentric babble — it is self-regulation in progress, later internalised as inner speech. This directly contradicts Piaget's view of egocentric speech.
    • Cultural tools (number systems, maps, writing) shape thought; hence cooperative/group learning and peer tutoring are Vygotskian classrooms.

    One-line contrast for the exam: Piaget = development precedes learning (maturation limits what teaching can do); Vygotsky = learning leads development (good teaching pulls development forward).

    Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD)

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    Kohlberg — stages of moral development

    Using dilemmas like the famous Heinz dilemma (should Heinz steal an overpriced drug to save his wife?), Kohlberg found reasoning — not the verdict — reveals the stage. Three levels, six stages:

    • Level 1 — Pre-conventional (up to ~9 yrs): Stage 1, obedience & punishment ("don't steal or you'll be punished"); Stage 2, instrumental/individualism ("I'll scratch your back if you scratch mine").
    • Level 2 — Conventional (~9 yrs–adolescence): Stage 3, "good boy/good girl" orientation (approval-seeking); Stage 4, law-and-order orientation (duty, rules maintain society).
    • Level 3 — Post-conventional (rare, some adults): Stage 5, social contract (laws serve justice and can be changed); Stage 6, universal ethical principles (conscience over law).

    Traps: a child obeying to avoid punishment is Stage 1; obeying because "rules must be followed" is Stage 4; stealing the drug because "life outweighs property" is Stage 5/6. Also: Kohlberg's stages are invariant and universal in sequence (critics dispute the universality — Carol Gilligan's ethic of care critique is occasionally asked).

    Kohlberg's 3 levels, 6 stages of moral development

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    Erikson — psychosocial development (8 stages)

    Each stage is a crisis; resolution builds a virtue. CTET focuses on the school-age stages:

    • Trust vs Mistrust (infancy), Autonomy vs Shame (toddlerhood), Initiative vs Guilt (preschool), Industry vs Inferiority (6–12 yrs — the primary-school stage: praise effort and competence, not just outcomes), Identity vs Role Confusion (adolescence).
    • Later stages (intimacy, generativity, integrity) appear rarely, usually as one matching item.

    Exam link: "A teacher praises a student's hard work so the child feels competent" tests Erikson's industry vs inferiority, not Skinner's reinforcement — read the stem's vocabulary before choosing.

    Rapid recall: Piaget — stages of thinking (schemas, conservation); Vygotsky — social learning (ZPD, scaffolding, MKO); Kohlberg — moral reasoning (Heinz, 3 levels/6 stages); Erikson — psychosocial crises (industry vs inferiority in primary years).

    2. Learning, Motivation & Pedagogy: Theories and Classroom Craft

    Gagné — nine events of instruction

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    Piaget vs Vygotsky — compare columns

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    This chapter covers the learning theories, motivation frameworks, and pedagogical tools that fill the remaining "learning and pedagogy" questions — behaviourist, cognitivist, and humanist theories, what actually motivates a child, and the teaching moves examiners reward.

    Behaviourist theories: observable change

    • Thorndike — trial and error; Laws of Learning: Law of Readiness (learn when ready/motivated), Law of Exercise (practice strengthens the connection), Law of Effect (satisfying consequences strengthen behaviour; annoying ones weaken it).
    • Pavlov — classical conditioning: learning by association (bell → salivation). Classroom link: a child anxious about maths after repeated humiliation has been "conditioned" — the cure is re-association, not scolding.
    • Skinner — operant conditioning: behaviour shaped by consequences. Positive reinforcement (adding praise), negative reinforcement (removing an unpleasant task when the child performs — not punishment), punishment (adding/removing to suppress). Schedules of reinforcement: continuous (every response — fastest learning) vs partial; among partial schedules, variable-ratio (unpredictable rewards, e.g. surprise praise) produces the most persistent behaviour. Trap: negative reinforcement increases desired behaviour by removing something aversive; students routinely confuse it with punishment.

    Cognitivist and social theories: the mind at work

    • Bruner — discovery learning & spiral curriculum: any subject can be taught in some honest form at any age; revisit concepts at increasing depth (the spiral). Three modes of representation: enactive (action-based), iconic (image-based), symbolic (language/symbols) — the direct ancestor of "concrete → pictorial → abstract" in maths pedagogy.
    • Ausubel — meaningful verbal learning: the single most important factor in learning is what the learner already knows. Advance organizers (introductory frameworks presented before the lesson) bridge prior knowledge to new material. Rote learning happens when material is arbitrary and unanchored.
    • Bandura — social (observational) learning: the Bobo doll experiments; learning through attention → retention → reproduction → motivation. Modelling matters — hence the teacher-as-role-model questions. Self-efficacy (belief in one's capability) is Bandura's too: a child with high self-efficacy persists longer.
    • Gardner — multiple intelligences: linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, bodily-kinesthetic, musical, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalistic (later: existential). Exam use: "A child weak in maths but brilliant at music" → MI theory argues against labelling the child unintelligent; teach through strengths.
    • Constructivism (Piaget/Vygotsky applied): learners build understanding; the teacher is a facilitator, not a transmitter. Constructivist classrooms: prior-knowledge elicitation, hands-on activity, collaborative problem-solving, reflection.

    Motivation: what moves the learner

    • Intrinsic vs extrinsic: curiosity and mastery (intrinsic) beat rewards and fear (extrinsic) for deep learning — but overuse of extrinsic rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation (the overjustification effect).
    • Maslow's hierarchy: physiological → safety → belongingness → esteem → self-actualization. A hungry or frightened child cannot attend to algebra — deficiency needs must be met first.
    • McClelland — achievement motivation (n-Ach): high achievers prefer moderately challenging tasks (50:50 success odds), personal responsibility, and feedback — useful for setting task difficulty.
    • Weiner — attribution theory: students explain success/failure by ability, effort, task difficulty, or luck. Teach effort attributions ("you succeeded because you worked at it") — ability attributions for failure ("I'm just bad at maths") destroy persistence. This is the theoretical engine behind growth mindset.
    • Locus of control (Rotter): internal ("my effort decides") vs external ("luck/teacher decides"); internal locus predicts persistence.

    Maslow's hierarchy — what moves the learner

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    Pedagogy: assessment, taxonomy, method

    • Bloom's revised taxonomy (Remember → Understand → Apply → Analyze → Evaluate → Create): CTET asks you to classify question stems — "design an experiment" is Create; "justify your answer" is Evaluate; "list the parts" is Remember. Aim classroom questions at the higher levels.
    • Formative vs summative assessment: formative is assessment for learning (ongoing feedback, quizzes, observations); summative is assessment of learning (term exams). Diagnostic assessment identifies specific difficulties before teaching. CCE (Continuous and Comprehensive Evaluation) weaves formative assessment through the year.
    • Teaching methods: lecture (efficient, passive), discussion, demonstration, project method (Kilpatrick — purposeful activity), problem-solving, play-way (Froebel — kindergarten), Montessori (self-directed, prepared environment, sensorial materials), Dalton Plan, heuristic method (Armstrong — discovery by the pupil). Match the method to the stem: "learning by doing purposeful activity" = project method; "children choose their own work in a prepared environment" = Montessori.
    • Common traps: (a) "learning styles" (VAK) have weak evidence — CTET rarely endorses labelling children; (b) intelligence is multi-faceted and malleable — avoid "IQ is fixed" distractors; (c) errors are windows into thinking (a constructivist view), not just mistakes to erase.

    Rapid recall: Reinforcement schedules — Skinner; advance organizers — Ausubel; spiral curriculum — Bruner; self-efficacy & modelling — Bandura; effort attributions — Weiner; 8 intelligences — Gardner; "what the learner already knows" — Ausubel; formative = for learning, summative = of learning.
