    3. Inclusive Education, NEP 2020 & the RTE Act

    From exclusion to inclusion — four models

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    Policy-and-rights questions are high-scoring because they are factual and finite: a fixed set of Acts, articles, and NEP provisions repeats across CTET and BPSC TRE papers. Learn the numbers cold.

    RTE Act, 2009 — the constitutional promise made law

    Article 21A (inserted by the 86th Amendment, 2002) makes free and compulsory education a fundamental right for children aged 6–14 years; the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 operationalises it (in force 1 April 2010).

    • Free and compulsory: no fees, no charges; the state must provide neighbourhood schooling. "Compulsory" binds the state, not the parent — a frequent trap.
    • 25% reservation in private unaided schools for children from economically weaker/disadvantaged sections (reimbursed by the state).
    • No detention policy: originally, no child could be failed till Class 8 — amended in 2019 to allow detention in Classes 5 and 8 after re-examination. Post-2019 questions test the amendment.
    • Prohibitions: no corporal punishment, no mental harassment, no screening tests/interviews for admission, no capitation fees.
    • Norms: prescribed pupil–teacher ratios (30:1 primary, 35:1 upper primary), infrastructure standards, School Management Committees (SMCs) with 75% parent membership, and trained teachers within the stipulated timeline.

    NEP 2020 — the new architecture

    • 5+3+3+4 structure replacing 10+2: Foundational (ages 3–8: 3 yrs preschool + Grades 1–2), Preparatory (8–11: Grades 3–5), Middle (11–14: Grades 6–8), Secondary (14–18: Grades 9–12).
    • ECCE universalisation: early childhood care and education for ages 3–6 brought inside the formal system (Balvatika/preparatory class); target GER 100% in preschool to secondary by 2030.
    • Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN): the NIPUN Bharat mission targets universal FLN by Grade 3.
    • Multilingualism: medium of instruction, wherever possible, in the home/local language till at least Grade 5, preferably till Grade 8; the three-language formula continues.
    • No hard separations between arts/science/commerce streams, curricular/extracurricular, vocational/academic; bagless days, coding from Grade 6 (as an exposure, not a mandate — read stems carefully).
    • Assessment reform: PARAKH as standard-setting body; board exams made easier, modular, twice-a-year offering; 360-degree holistic report cards.
    • Teachers: 4-year integrated B.Ed as the minimum teaching degree by 2030; restoration of teacher dignity, merit-based postings, and continuous professional development.
    • Gross Enrolment Ratio targets: 100% preschool–secondary, 50% higher education by 2035; 6% of GDP as the (long-standing, still aspirational) education spending target.
    • Trap: NEP 2020 is a policy, not a law — it guides; the RTE Act is enforceable legislation. Questions mixing the two test exactly this distinction.

    NEP 2020 — the 5+3+3+4 architecture

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    Inclusive education: every child in the mainstream classroom

    Inclusion means educating children with special needs in regular classrooms with support — it is not "integration" (placing them in but expecting them to cope) and not segregation (separate schools).

    • RPwD Act, 2016: replaced the 1995 Act; recognises 21 specified disabilities (up from 7); reservation in government jobs raised from 3% to 4%; free education for children with benchmark disabilities (6–18 yrs). CTET asks the count: 21.
    • Specific learning disabilities: dyslexia (reading — letter reversals, slow decoding), dysgraphia (writing — illegible handwriting, spacing), dyscalculia (number sense, arithmetic), dyspraxia (motor coordination). Classroom moves: extra time, oral testing options, multi-sensory input, chunked instructions — never ridicule or lowered expectations disguised as pity.
    • ADHD: inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity — seat near the teacher, short tasks, movement breaks, clear routines.
    • Autism Spectrum Disorder: social-communication differences, restricted/repetitive behaviours — visual schedules, predictable routines, sensory sensitivity awareness.
    • Gifted/talented children also need inclusion: enrichment, not just acceleration — open-ended tasks, mentorship, independent projects. Boredom misread as misbehaviour is the classic exam vignette.
    • Gender, caste, and language inclusion: inclusive classrooms use gender-neutral language, diverse examples, mother-tongue bridging, and zero tolerance for stereotyping ("boys are better at maths" is the distractor CTET expects you to reject).
    • Reasonable accommodations: assistive technology, scribes, large print, peer buddies, flexible seating — and IEPs (Individualised Education Plans) for children with significant needs.

    Numbers to memorise: RTE — ages 6–14, 25% reservation, 30:1 / 35:1 PTR; NEP — 5+3+3+4, mother tongue till Grade 5 (preferably 8), FLN by Grade 3, 4-yr integrated B.Ed by 2030, GER 50% higher-ed by 2035; RPwD — 21 disabilities, 4% job reservation; Article 21A — 86th Amendment, 2002.

    4. EVS Content & Pedagogy: Themes, Concepts, Classroom Practice

    EVS — six NCERT themes

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    EVS (Classes 3–5, NCERT) is taught as an integrated subject — not science + social science side by side, but one lens on the child's environment. CTET Paper I tests both content (the facts children must learn) and pedagogy (how EVS must be taught).

    Why EVS exists: NCF 2005 aims

    • Train children to locate and comprehend relationships between the natural, social, and cultural environment.
    • Develop observation, classification, and inference through lived experience — EVS is the foundation of scientific temper.
    • Nurture curiosity, creativity, and environmental sensitivity; connect classroom learning to life outside school.
    • Cover six NCERT themes: Family and Friends; Food; Shelter; Water; Travel; Things We Make and Do. (Examiners occasionally ask which topic belongs to which theme — e.g. "pottery" → Things We Make and Do; "migration for work" → Travel.)

    Core content clusters

    • Our body and health: sense organs and their care, balanced diet, food nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals), deficiency awareness, personal hygiene, common illnesses and prevention.
    • Plants and animals: parts of plants and their functions, germination needs (air, water, warmth), habitats, herbivores/carnivores/omnivores, food chains (grass → goat → human; know the direction of energy flow), endangered species basics, care of animals.
    • Water: sources (rain, rivers, wells, handpumps), the water cycle (evaporation → condensation → precipitation → collection), states of water, water pollution causes, conservation practices (rainwater harvesting, drip irrigation), traditional systems like stepwells.
    • Air, soil, seasons: composition of air in simple terms, uses of air, types of soil and crops suited to them, the three Indian seasons and associated festivals/clothing/food.
    • Shelter and neighbourhood: types of houses (kutcha/pucca, stilt houses in Assam, houseboats in Kashmir — regional adaptation to climate), neighbourhood services (post office, hospital, police station), community helpers and dignity of labour.
    • Travel and transport: modes of transport (land, water, air), tickets and fares, mapping skills (directions, symbols, scale — the Class 5 mapping unit), journeys and migration.
    • Things we make and do: fibres to fabric (cotton, jute, silk, wool), pottery, farming steps, tools and occupations.

    EVS pedagogy: how it must be taught

    • Experiential and activity-based: field trips, nature walks, surveys (e.g. "survey water sources in your locality"), simple experiments (germination in a transparent jar, filtration with cloth), observation records. "A teacher takes children to a pond to observe aquatic life" is textbook EVS pedagogy.
    • Start from the child's immediate environment and expand outward: self → family → neighbourhood → state → country → world. Abstract definitions before experience is the anti-pattern.
    • Questioning: open-ended, divergent questions ("Why do you think the leaves turned yellow?") over recall questions; encourage children to ask their own questions — curiosity is a learning objective.
    • Addressing misconceptions: elicit prior ideas first (many children think "the sun moves across the sky" or "plants eat soil"); confront gently with evidence, don't lecture them away.
    • CCE in EVS: assess through observation, portfolios, drawings, group tasks, and oral expression — not only written tests. Process (how the child investigated) counts alongside product.
    • Storytelling and role play: narratives, folk tales, and role-play of community helpers make abstract social concepts concrete for young learners — a staple of NCERT EVS textbooks (the Class 3–5 books are built around stories).
    • Values integration: sensitivity towards the environment and living beings, respect for manual work, gender equity in roles — EVS carries the affective curriculum.

    Traps: (a) EVS is integrated, not a merger of separate science/SST periods; (b) the water cycle order and food-chain direction are the two most-asked factual items; (c) any stem with "rote memorisation of definitions" as the teaching method is the wrong option in EVS pedagogy — experience-first always wins.

    5. Mathematics Content & Pedagogy: Concepts, Methods, Misconceptions

    CPA approach — three stages

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    Mathematics pedagogy questions reward teachers who know why children get sums wrong. The pattern is consistent: a classroom vignette, a child's error, and four candidate teacher responses — the constructivist response (diagnose the thinking, use concrete material, let the child reconstruct) is almost always correct.

    Core content: what Classes 1–5 must master

    • Number system and place value: counting, number names, Indian place-value (ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, lakhs), expanded form, comparing and ordering numbers, odd/even, prime/composite (upper primary). Place-value misunderstanding is the root of most arithmetic errors.
    • Four operations: addition, subtraction, multiplication, division — with meaning, not just algorithms. "12 ÷ 3" as sharing (12 sweets among 3 children) and as grouping (how many 3s in 12); multiplication as repeated addition and as arrays/area.
    • Fractions and decimals: fraction as part of a whole, part of a collection, and as division; equivalent fractions, comparing, addition/subtraction of like fractions; decimals as an extension of place value (tenths, hundredths). Classic misconception: treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers (claiming 1/4 > 1/3 because 4 > 3).
    • Measurement: length (cm, m, km), weight (g, kg), capacity (ml, l), time (reading clocks, calendar, 24-hour basics), money (rupees-paise, bills and change). Estimation before exact measurement is the pedagogical point.
    • Geometry: 2D shapes (properties of triangles, quadrilaterals, circles), 3D shapes (cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere — faces, edges, vertices), symmetry (line of symmetry, mirror images), patterns and tessellation.
    • Data handling: pictographs, bar graphs, tally marks — reading and drawing simple representations; "which month had the most rainfall?" style interpretation.
    • Patterns: number patterns, shape patterns, growing patterns — the bridge to algebraic thinking.

    Pedagogy: how maths must be taught

    • Concrete → Pictorial → Abstract (CPA): Bruner's enactive–iconic–symbolic in maths dress. Teach place value with bundles of sticks before numerals; fractions with paper folding before symbols. Skipping straight to the algorithm is the standard wrong option.
    • Van Hiele levels of geometric thought: Level 0 Visualization (recognising shapes by appearance), Level 1 Analysis (noticing properties), Level 2 Abstraction/Informal deduction (relating properties — "a square is a rectangle"), Level 3 Deduction, Level 4 Rigor. Primary teaching lives at Levels 0–1: sorting, building, and describing shapes — not formal proofs.
    • Problem-solving — Polya's four steps: understand the problem, devise a plan, carry out the plan, look back (verify). Teach the process, not just the answer.
    • Constructivist maths classroom: pose real problems, let children invent strategies, discuss multiple methods ("how many ways can we solve 25 × 12?"), use manipulatives (abacus, number line, base-ten blocks, tangrams, geoboards).
    • Error analysis: treat errors diagnostically. A child writing 503 − 278 = 385 has a borrowing misconception — re-teach with concrete regrouping, don't just mark it wrong. "Ask the child to explain their thinking" beats "give ten more sums for practice" in every CTET key.
    • Maths anxiety and attitude: timed speed tests and public humiliation create fear; games, puzzles, and low-floor-high-ceiling tasks build confidence. NCF 2005's twin goals — mathematisation of thought (thinking mathematically about the world) and narrowing the gap between school maths and children's out-of-school mathematical thinking.
    • Assessment in maths: formative — observation of strategy, oral explanation, open-ended tasks ("make three different rectangles with area 24"); avoid over-testing rote tables as a proxy for understanding.
    • Language of maths: precise vocabulary (sum, difference, product, quotient, numerator, perimeter vs area) taught through use; word problems test comprehension as much as computation — let children pose their own problems too.

    Traps: (a) a child getting the right answer with the wrong method still needs the method corrected — understanding is the goal; (b) drill has a place after concept formation, never before; (c) "mathematics is only for the intelligent" is the distractor to reject — NCF 2005 insists every child can learn meaningful mathematics; (d) Van Hiele Level 0 is visualization, not proof.

    6. Science Content & Pedagogy

    Scientific method — seven steps

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    What the examiner really tests

    CTET Paper II science questions split into two layers: core concepts (roughly NCERT Class 6–8 science) and how science should be taught. The pedagogy half is where most marks are lost, because it rewards one idea above all — science is a way of investigating, not a list of facts to recite. Whenever a question asks what the teacher should do first, the answer is almost never "explain the definition" but "let learners observe, predict or test."

    Nature of science: the non-negotiables

    • Science is empirical and tentative. Conclusions rest on evidence and can change with new evidence. A statement that can never be tested is not science.
    • Observation is theory-laden. Two students can watch the same burning candle and notice different things. The teacher's job is to make observations sharper, not to hand over "the correct observation."
    • Process and product both matter. Facts, concepts, laws and theories are the product; observing, classifying, measuring, hypothesizing, controlling variables, interpreting data and communicating are the process skills — and pedagogy questions test the process skills more.
    • No single "scientific method" recipe. The textbook steps (hypothesis → experiment → conclusion) are a simplification. Question the option that treats them as a rigid ritual.

    The 5E model (inquiry-based teaching)

    Engage – Explore – Explain – Elaborate – Evaluate. In an exam vignette, the teacher who begins with a puzzling demo or a discrepant event (a raw egg dropped in salt water floating, a balloon that won't pop on nails) is at Engage; students handling materials themselves are at Explore; only after that does the teacher formalize the concept (Explain), extend it to new situations (Elaborate) and check understanding (Evaluate). Any option that jumps to definitions before exploration contradicts the model.

    The 5E model — inquiry-based teaching cycle

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    High-yield content spine (Classes 6–8 level)

    • Motion & force: speed = distance ÷ time; uniform vs non-uniform motion; friction opposes relative motion but enables walking, gripping and braking; a force can change shape, speed or direction. Trap: "heavier objects fall faster" — in free fall (ignoring air resistance) all objects accelerate equally.
    • Energy: kinetic + potential; energy transforms (chemical → heat → light in a candle) and is conserved; simple machines reduce effort, not work.
    • Matter: particle spacing and motion explain solid/liquid/gas; melting/boiling points; physical vs chemical change (a chemical change makes a new substance — rusting, burning, curdling); acids turn blue litmus red, bases turn red litmus blue; neutralization gives salt + water.
    • Electricity & magnetism: current needs a closed circuit; series shares current, parallel branches share voltage; like poles repel; the Earth's magnetism and electromagnets.
    • Light & sound: light travels in straight lines (shadows, eclipses); reflection laws; sound needs a medium — it cannot travel through vacuum (classic trap); pitch depends on frequency.
    • Living world: cell is the structural and functional unit; photosynthesis (light energy → chemical energy, oxygen released — test with a leaf decolourised and iodine); respiration releases energy; transport in plants (xylem/phloem) and animals (circulation); reproduction in plants — vegetative, sexual; seed dispersal agents.
    • Environment: food chains/webs; decomposers recycle nutrients; greenhouse effect vs global warming (related, not identical); water cycle stages.

    Classic misconceptions to expect as distractors

    • Seasons are caused by the Earth being closer to the Sun (actually: axial tilt).
    • Plants get their food from the soil (they make it; soil supplies water and minerals).
    • Boiling water keeps getting hotter after it boils (temperature stays constant at boiling point).
    • Clouds are made of water vapour (visible clouds are tiny liquid droplets; vapour is invisible).
    • The Moon gives off its own light (it reflects sunlight).

    Pedagogy: the recurring patterns

    • Predict–Observe–Explain (POE): ask for a prediction before the demo; the clash between prediction and observation is where learning happens.
    • Fair test: change one variable, control the rest, measure the outcome. Questions often ask what is wrong with a described experiment — look for the uncontrolled variable.
    • Low-cost/no-cost materials: the NCF-2005 position paper on science expects experiments with everyday materials; an option requiring an expensive lab set-up is usually the wrong pedagogy.
    • Field visits and projects: preferred over "extra homework" for topics like biodiversity or water.
    • Assessment: test process skills (design a test, interpret a table) alongside content; avoid questions that only reward recall of definitions.
    Examiner trap: "The teacher demonstrates the experiment while students watch and note the result" sounds efficient, but any option where students themselves manipulate variables outranks it on inquiry questions.

    7. Social Science Content

    Sources of history — the tree

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    How the paper is built

    CTET Paper II social science covers History, Geography, Social & Political Life (civics) and a slice of Economics — roughly NCERT Classes 6–8 (with some 9–10 spillover in civics). Questions test content accuracy plus pedagogy of evidence: using sources, maps and timelines rather than memorizing dates. BPSC TRE subject papers go deeper into the same spine, with a Bihar weightage (ancient centres of learning, the freedom movement in Bihar, state geography).

    History: anchor points, not date lists

    • Sources: archaeological (inscriptions, coins, monuments, artefacts), literary (texts, manuscripts) and oral traditions. Key examiner point: every source reflects a perspective and a context — inscriptions, for instance, record what rulers wanted remembered. Teach source criticism, not source worship.
    • Harappan civilization: planned towns (grid pattern, drainage), standardised weights, seals — evidence of trade and craft specialization. Trap: Harappans did not build large temples/palaces like later periods; avoid projecting later features backward.
    • Vedic period → Mahajanapadas → Mauryas: iron and agriculture's role in state formation; Ashoka's dhamma (policy of moral conduct, not a religion) and his edicts as a source.
    • Early medieval: Bhakti and Sufi movements as social reform currents; temple architecture and regional kingdoms.
    • Delhi Sultanate → Mughals: administrative systems (iqta, mansabdari), Akbar's policies of sulh-i-kul, economic life. Trap: do not confuse the Sultanate's five dynasties' order.
    • Colonial period: revenue systems (Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari, Mahalwari — who paid whom is the testable part), deindustrialization debates, the Revolt of 1857 (multiple causes, multiple centres), social reformers.
    • Freedom movement: moderates–extremists–Gandhian phases; Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Quit India; Champaran Satyagraha (1917) — Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, against the tinkathia system in indigo cultivation (high Bihar weightage); JP's role in the Quit India movement; the role of women, peasants and workers.

    Geography: concepts that recur

    • The Earth: rotation (day/night) vs revolution (seasons, with axial tilt as the cause); latitudes (Equator, Tropics, Arctic/Antarctic circles) and longitudes (Prime Meridian; local time changes ~4 minutes per degree — a favourite calculation).
    • Interior & landforms: crust–mantle–core; weathering vs erosion; work of rivers, wind and glaciers; mountains, plateaus, plains.
    • Climate: the monsoon as a seasonal reversal of winds, not merely "heavy rain"; factors of climate — latitude, altitude, distance from sea, winds.
    • Resources: renewable vs non-renewable; conservation vs sustainable development; water, forests, minerals — map-based questions on Indian rivers, soils and crops are staples.
    • India: location and size, physical divisions, drainage (Himalayan vs peninsular rivers — perennial vs seasonal), agriculture types, industries and population.

    Civics: the Constitution spine

    • Preamble: sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic, republic — plus justice, equality, liberty, fraternity. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added "socialist, secular, integrity".
    • Fundamental Rights vs Directive Principles: rights are justiciable (enforceable by courts); DPSPs are non-justiciable guidelines for the state. Classic trap: Right to Property is now a legal right (Article 300A), not a Fundamental Right.
    • Organs of government: legislature–executive–judiciary; separation of powers; Parliament (Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha) and state legislatures.
    • Federalism & local government: Union, State and Concurrent lists; the 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) constitutionalised Panchayati Raj and urban local bodies — reservations including for women.
    • Democracy & diversity: elections and the Election Commission; secularism as principled distance (Indian model — not strict separation); understanding marginalisation and the role of government in health and education.

    Economics essentials

    • Needs vs wants; goods vs services; primary–secondary–tertiary sectors; organised vs unorganised sector; the role of the public sector.
    • Poverty, unemployment types (seasonal, disguised — especially in agriculture), and basic ideas of development (per capita income's limits; HDI as a broader measure).

    Social science pedagogy: what the examiner rewards

    • Multiple sources, multiple perspectives: a textbook account of a battle next to a folk song about it — then ask what each emphasises.
    • Maps and timelines as thinking tools: students plotting the Revolt of 1857's centres on a map learn more than from a list.
    • Role-play and mock institutions: a mock panchayat or parliament makes abstract civics concrete.
    • Connect to the present: link historical events to contemporary issues (e.g., water disputes → federalism; market visit → sectors of economy).
    • Assessment: map-pointing, source-based questions, short argumentative answers ("Give two reasons…") — never only one-mark dates.
    Examiner trap: an option that presents a single textbook narrative as "the complete truth" is usually wrong in social science pedagogy; the right answer honours evidence, perspective and debate.

    8. Hindi Bhasha Shikshan (हिंदी भाषा शिक्षण)

    भाषा की प्रकृति: परीक्षा की नींव

    • भाषा अर्जन बनाम अधिगम: मातृभाषा अर्जित होती है — सहज, अनौपचारिक परिवेश में; द्वितीय भाषा कक्षा में सीखी जाती है। क्रैशन (Krashen) के अनुसार अर्थपूर्ण निवेश (comprehensible input, i+1) और निम्न भावात्मक फ़िल्टर (कम डर/तनाव) अधिग्रहण की शर्तें हैं।
    • NCF-2005 की भाषा-शिक्षा संबंधी स्थिति: मातृभाषा/घर की भाषा प्राथमिक स्तर पर माध्यम हो; त्रिभाषा सूत्र (हिंदी, अंग्रेज़ी + एक आधुनिक भारतीय/विदेशी भाषा); भाषा केवल विषय नहीं, सभी विषयों के अधिगम का माध्यम है।
    • त्रुटियाँ सीखने की सीढ़ी हैं — दंड का नहीं, निदान का विषय। बहुभाषिक कक्षा में बच्चे की घरेलू भाषा संसाधन है, बाधा नहीं।

    भाषा-शिक्षण की प्रमुख विधियाँ

    • व्याकरण-अनुवाद विधि: नियम पहले, फिर अनुवाद; पठन-लेखन पर बल, बोलने की उपेक्षा। रटंत-प्रधान — आधुनिक प्रश्नों में प्रायः नकारात्मक विकल्प।
    • प्रत्यक्ष विधि (Direct Method): लक्ष्य भाषा में ही शिक्षण, अनुवाद निषेध; मौखिक कौशल पर बल।
    • द्विभाषी विधि: मातृभाषा का सीमित, सोद्देश्य प्रयोग कठिन अंशों को स्पष्ट करने हेतु।
    • संरचनात्मक उपागम: वाक्य-संरचनाओं (patterns) का क्रमिक अभ्यास — "यह कलम है / यह किताब है"।
    • संप्रेषणात्मक उपागम (CLT): भाषा का उद्देश्य संप्रेषण; गतिविधि-आधारित, युग्म/समूह कार्य; त्रुटि से अधिक संदेश की सफलता महत्त्वपूर्ण।

    चार कौशल (LSRW) और उनका क्रम

    श्रवण → वाचन (बोलना) → पठन → लेखन। श्रवण में ध्यानपूर्वक सुनना, भाव ग्रहण; वाचन में शुद्ध उच्चारण, प्रवाह; पठन के प्रकार — गहन पठन (विस्तृत समझ) व विस्तृत/द्रुत पठन (सार ग्रहण, स्किमिंग-स्कैनिंग); लेखन में वर्तनी, विराम-चिह्न, अनुच्छेद-रचना। व्याकरण पढ़ाने की आगमन विधि (उदाहरण → नियम) निगमन विधि (नियम → उदाहरण) से श्रेष्ठ मानी जाती है।

    हिंदी व्याकरण: अति-महत्त्वपूर्ण खंड

    • संधि: दो वर्णों के मेल से परिवर्तन — स्वर संधि (विद्या + आलय = विद्यालय), व्यंजन संधि (उत् + चारण = उच्चारण), विसर्ग संधि (मनः + रथ = मनोरथ)।
    • समास: अव्ययीभाव (यथाशक्ति — पहला पद प्रधान), तत्पुरुष (राजकुमार = राजा का कुमार — दूसरा पद प्रधान, कारक-लोप), कर्मधारय (नीलकमल — विशेषण-विशेष्य), द्विगु (त्रिभुवन — पहला पद संख्यावाची), द्वन्द्व (माता-पिता — दोनों पद प्रधान, 'और' का लोप), बहुव्रीहि (चतुर्भुज — तीसरा अर्थ प्रधान, 'विष्णु')। पहचान-सूत्र: विग्रह करके देखें — कौन-सा पद प्रधान है?
    • उपसर्ग (शब्द के पहले: प्र + हार = प्रहार) व प्रत्यय (शब्द के बाद: लड़ + आई = लड़ाई)।
    • कारक (8): कर्ता (ने), कर्म (को), करण (से — साधन), संप्रदान (के लिए), अपादान (से — अलग होना), संबंध (का/की/के), अधिकरण (में/पर), संबोधन (हे!/अरे!)। जाल: करण और अपादान दोनों में 'से' — साधन हो तो करण, पृथकता हो तो अपादान।
    • वाच्य (3): कर्तृवाच्य (मोहन पत्र लिखता है), कर्मवाच्य (पत्र मोहन द्वारा लिखा जाता है), भाववाच्य (मुझसे चला नहीं जाता)।
    • अव्यय: क्रियाविशेषण, संबंधबोधक, समुच्चयबोधक, विस्मयादिबोधक — लिंग-वचन से अप्रभावित।
    • शब्द-भंडार: पर्यायवाची, विलोम, अनेकार्थी, श्रुतिसम भिन्नार्थक (अन्न-अन्य), अनेक शब्दों के लिए एक शब्द।
    • मुहावरा बनाम लोकोक्ति: मुहावरा वाक्यांश है (वाक्य में प्रयोग से पूर्ण — "नौ दो ग्यारह होना"), लोकोक्ति पूर्ण वाक्य व स्वतंत्र सत्य ("जैसी करनी वैसी भरनी")।
    • रस, छंद, अलंकार (संक्षेप): रस 9 (शृंगार, हास्य, करुण, रौद्र, वीर, भयानक, वीभत्स, अद्भुत, शांत); अलंकार — उपमा ("सा/जैसा"), रूपक (अभेद), उत्प्रेक्षा ("मानो"), अतिशयोक्ति, यमक, श्लेष।

    आकलन और गद्यांश-युक्तियाँ

    • सतत एवं समग्र मूल्यांकन: पठन-वाचन-श्रवण-लेखन का अवलोकन, पोर्टफ़ोलियो, उपचारात्मक शिक्षण। केवल वर्तनी-त्रुटि पर अंक काटना संकीर्ण आकलन है।
    • गद्यांश/पद्यांश: पहले प्रश्न पढ़ें, फिर गद्यांश — उत्तर पाठ के भीतर खोजें, बाहरी ज्ञान से नहीं। शीर्षक हेतु केंद्रीय भाव चुनें।
    • वर्तनी व विराम-चिह्न: श्रुतलेख (dictation) वर्तनी सुधार का प्रभावी साधन है; पूर्ण विराम, प्रश्नवाचक, अल्पविराम का प्रयोग-आधारित अभ्यास कराएँ — नियम रटाने से नहीं, वाक्य-रचना के साथ।
    • पठन-पूर्व गतिविधि: पाठ शुरू करने से पहले चित्र-चर्चा या पूर्वज्ञान प्रश्न — इससे पठन सोद्देश्य और रुचिकर होता है।
    Examiner trap: जिस विकल्प में शिक्षक पहले नियम लिखवाए फिर उदाहरण दे (निगमन), वह आगमन-विधि वाले विकल्प से हारता है; और "शुद्धता के लिए बच्चे को बीच में टोकना" संप्रेषणात्मक कक्षा में गलत माना जाता है।

    9. English Language & Pedagogy

    Methods of teaching English — four compared

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    Theories the examiner loves

    • Skinner (Behaviourist): language learned through imitation, repetition and reinforcement — habit formation. Explains drills, not creativity.
    • Chomsky (Innatist): children are born with a Language Acquisition Device (LAD); they generate sentences they never heard — proof that language is not mere imitation.
    • Krashen: Acquisition (subconscious, like the mother tongue) vs learning (conscious rules); Input Hypothesis — we acquire from comprehensible input at level i+1; Affective Filter — anxiety blocks acquisition, so a low-stress classroom matters.
    • Vygotsky: learning is social; the Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) is the gap between what a child can do alone and with help — scaffolding (hints, modelling, peer support) bridges it, then is withdrawn.

    Approaches and methods

    • Grammar–Translation: rules first, translation exercises; strong on reading/writing, weak on speaking — the "traditional" option examiners contrast against.
    • Direct Method: only the target language in class; meaning through demonstration, not translation.
    • Audio-lingual: pattern drills and dialogues; behaviourist roots; accuracy through repetition.
    • Communicative Language Teaching (CLT): fluency and real communication; pair/group work, role-play, information-gap tasks; errors tolerated when meaning succeeds.
    • Task-Based Language Teaching (TBLT): language learned by doing — plan a trip, solve a problem — with a language focus after the task.
    • Eclectic approach: the wise-teacher answer — choosing methods to suit learners, never one method for all situations.

    Skills: LSRW and sub-skills

    • Listening: discriminating sounds, listening for gist vs specific information; dictation and storytelling build it.
    • Speaking: pronunciation (stress, intonation), fluency before accuracy in early stages; drills → guided → free practice.
    • Reading: skimming (gist), scanning (specific detail), intensive (close study), extensive (longer texts for pleasure — builds vocabulary fastest).
    • Writing: controlled → guided → free writing; process approach — plan, draft, revise, edit. Mechanics (spelling, punctuation) serve meaning, not the reverse.
    • Receptive (listening, reading) vs productive (speaking, writing) — a favourite one-mark distinction.

    Grammar core (error-spotting territory)

    • Subject–verb agreement: the verb follows the true head noun — "The quality of the apples is good." Neither/either take singular verbs.
    • Tenses: all twelve, but the exam lives on present perfect vs simple past ("I have seen it" vs "I saw it yesterday") and since/for ("since Monday", "for three days").
    • Voice: object → subject + be + past participle; "The work was completed by her."
    • Narration: past reporting verb shifts tenses back; universal truths don't shift ("He said the sun rises in the east").
    • Conditionals: Type 1 (will), Type 2 (would + past — unreal present), Type 3 (would have + past perfect — unreal past).
    • Articles & prepositions: "a university" (sound, not letter); preposition + time/place collocations (arrive at 6, in June, on Monday).
    • Common traps: much/many, few/a few, affect (verb)/effect (noun), its/it's, their/there/they're, "one of the boys is", question tags matching the auxiliary ("She can swim, can't she?").

    Vocabulary and the multilingual classroom

    • Word formation — prefixes, suffixes, compounding; collocations ("make a decision", not "do a decision"); homophones/homonyms.
    • A child's home language is a resource: allow translanguaging (moving between languages to make meaning) rather than banning it. Errors are developmental — diagnose the pattern (e.g., overgeneralising "-ed") instead of merely marking wrong.
    • Remedial teaching follows diagnosis; it is targeted re-teaching, not "more homework".
    • Error vs mistake: an error reflects a gap in competence (systematic, needs teaching); a mistake is a performance slip the learner can self-correct. Remedial plans target errors.
    • Integrated skills: real tasks blend skills — listen to a story, discuss it, then write an ending. Exam vignettes reward integration over isolated drills.

    Assessment of language

    • Test all four skills, not just grammar; use formative tools — observation checklists, reading records, portfolios of writing drafts.
    • Comprehension questions: literal (in the text), inferential (between the lines), evaluative (beyond the text). Good papers include all three.
    Examiner trap: "Correct every error immediately so it doesn't fossilise" loses to "note recurring errors and address the pattern later" — interrupting kills fluency and raises the affective filter.

    10. ICT, Assessment & Classroom Management

    Classroom management — three styles

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    ICT in the classroom: beyond the projector

    • TPACK: effective teaching sits at the overlap of content knowledge, pedagogy and technology. Technology that doesn't serve a learning goal is decoration.
    • SAMR ladder: Substitution (PDF instead of a printed page — no functional change) → Augmentation (quiz app with instant feedback) → Modification (students co-edit a document, peer-comment) → Redefinition (a class publishes a podcast for a real audience — impossible without tech). Exam vignettes ask which level a described activity reaches.
    • What works: simulations for invisible processes (water cycle, electric circuits), virtual manipulatives in maths, audio stories for language listening, formative quiz tools with instant feedback.
    • National digital backbone (know the names): DIKSHA — NCERT's platform for school digital resources; PM eVidya — the umbrella programme for digital/online education. Questions usually test recognition, not detail.
    • Cautions: the digital divide (device and connectivity gaps), screen-time balance, data privacy of learners, and the trap of "technology as reward" (free browsing time) instead of technology as learning.

    Assessment: purposes and types

    • Diagnostic: before teaching — finds gaps and misconceptions.
    • Formative (assessment for learning): during teaching — exit slips, questioning, observation; its feedback changes the next lesson. The highest-weightage concept in pedagogy sections.
    • Summative (assessment of learning): after teaching — term exams; judges achievement.
    • Norm-referenced (compare with peers — ranks) vs criterion-referenced (compare with fixed standards — pass marks).
    • CCE (Continuous and Comprehensive Evaluation): the RTE-era framework — continuous (spread across the term, not one final exam) and comprehensive (scholastic + co-scholastic: attitudes, values, life skills). Formative and summative tools both feed it.

    Assessment — diagnostic, formative, summative

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    Tools of assessment

    • Rubrics: criteria + performance levels described in words; shared with students before the task. Beats vague "good effort" marking.
    • Portfolios: a curated collection showing growth over time — strongest for writing and projects.
    • Anecdotal records & checklists: brief dated observations of behaviour or skills — the backbone of early-grade assessment.
    • Question design: match items to purpose. MCQ trap: distractors must be plausible; "all of the above" and grammatical giveaways weaken the item. Essay-type items test organization and argument, not just recall.

    Bloom's revised taxonomy (verbs matter)

    Remember → Understand → Apply → Analyze → Evaluate → Create. "Define" and "list" sit at Remember; "explain" and "summarise" at Understand; "solve using" at Apply; "compare the causes" at Analyze; "judge which is better" at Evaluate; "design" and "compose" at Create. Exam questions frequently ask you to classify an item — look at the verb.

    Feedback that teaches

    • Descriptive ("Your introduction states the claim clearly; the second paragraph needs one piece of evidence") beats evaluative ("Good!" / "Careless!").
    • Feedback must be timely, specific and actionable — and the learner must get a chance to use it (re-draft, retry).

    Classroom management

    • Prevention over reaction: clear routines (entry, distribution of materials, transitions), posted rules made with students, and brisk pacing prevent most misbehaviour.
    • Withitness (Kounin): the teacher's communicated awareness of everything happening in the room — scanning, naming, proximity — deters disruption better than punishment.
    • Positive discipline: natural/logical consequences over humiliation or corporal punishment (prohibited under RTE); reinforce the behaviour you want to see.
    • Time-on-task: engaged learning time is the strongest classroom predictor of achievement — manage transitions tightly.
    • Multi-grade and inclusive management: common in Indian primary schools — use peer tutoring, learning corners and self-directed task cards so one group works independently while the teacher instructs another.
    • Handling disruption: private, low-profile correction first; involve the student in solutions; escalate (parents, counsellor) only after classroom strategies fail.
    Examiner trap: "Send the disruptive child out of class so others can learn" feels efficient but loses to keeping the child engaged with a task — exclusion is the last resort, never the first step.

    11. Bihar General Studies for BPSC TRE

    Ancient Bihar: the heartland of empires and learning

    • Magadha and Pataliputra: ancient Magadha covered much of present-day south Bihar. Its capital Pataliputra (modern Patna) was the Mauryan and later Gupta administrative centre — the political heart of India for nearly a thousand years.
    • Buddhist councils: the first council met at Rajgir (Saptaparni cave) and the third at Pataliputra under Ashoka. Vaishali's Lichchhavi republic is counted among the world's earliest republican states — a favourite one-liner.
    • Nalanda and Vikramashila: Nalanda Mahavihara flourished from the 5th century CE under Gupta patronage, drawing scholars from across Asia; Vikramashila was founded by the Pala king Dharmapala. Both were destroyed in the 12th–13th centuries. The Nalanda archaeological site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2016).
    • Bodh Gaya: the Buddha attained enlightenment here; the Mahabodhi Temple became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002.
    • Ashokan rock-cut architecture: the Barabar caves near Gaya carry some of India's oldest rock-cut chambers, associated with the Mauryan period.

    Medieval and modern Bihar

    • Sher Shah Suri: founder of the Sur Empire (interregnum 1540–1555), belonged to Sasaram in Bihar; remembered for administrative reforms, the Grand Trunk Road and the rupiya.
    • Guru Gobind Singh: born in Patna in 1666; Takht Sri Harmandir Sahib, Patna Sahib marks the site — one of the five Sikh takhts.
    • Champaran Satyagraha (1917): Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, against the tinkathia system forcing indigo cultivation. Treat 1917 as an anchor date for Bihar's freedom movement.
    • Leaders: Dr Rajendra Prasad (first President of India, born in Ziradei), Jayaprakash Narayan (born in Sitabdiara; leader of the 1974 movement), and Sri Krishna Sinha — Bihar's first Chief Minister.
    • Bihar Day: 22 March marks Bihar's separation as a province from Bengal in 1912.

    Geography: rivers, plains and risk

    • The Ganga enters Bihar at Chausa (Buxar) and flows east across the state; the Sone joins it near Patna and the Gandak drains north Bihar.
    • The Kosi is called the 'Sorrow of Bihar' for its shifting course and devastating floods — a near-certain one-liner.
    • Protected areas: Valmiki National Park in West Champaran is Bihar's only national park and tiger reserve; the Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary near Bhagalpur protects the Gangetic dolphin.
    • Waterfalls and hills: Kakolat waterfall (Nawada) and the Rajgir hills are standard map-pointing facts.
    • Agriculture: the Gangetic alluvial plains make Bihar a major producer of rice, wheat, maize, pulses and litchi (Muzaffarpur's Shahi litchi holds a GI tag).

    Polity and administration

    • 38 districts grouped into 9 divisions; the Patna High Court was established in 1916.
    • Representation: 243 seats in the Legislative Assembly, 40 Lok Sabha seats and 16 Rajya Sabha seats.
    • State symbols: animal — gaur; bird — house sparrow; tree — peepal; flower — kachnar.
    • Literacy: 63.82% in Census 2011 — often asked alongside the national figure.
    • Current administration (know the mechanisms, not just names): the e-Shikshakosh portal records teachers' online attendance; the Shikshak Samadhan portal handles teachers' service grievances with a 30-day resolution target; the teacher rationalisation/transfer exercise of 2026 (around 42,000 surplus teachers in the provisional stage, completion targeted by 31 October 2026) tests how you follow education administration as current affairs.

    Bihar's teaching exams: the numbers that matter

    • BPSC TRE 4.0 (2026): 32,388 posts from primary to senior secondary; applications 25 September–26 October 2026 (fee by 25 October). Previous TRE cycles routinely appear in exam GA.
    • Bihar STET 2026: CBT, 150 MCQs for 150 marks in 2.5 hours, separate papers for Classes 9–10 and 11–12; dummy admit card with correction window is the standard pre-exam ritual — know what a 'dummy admit card' is for.
    • SCERT–Google MoU (2026): AI-powered tools and training for government school teachers — file under education technology, a growing exam theme.
    • How to study this chapter: make a 38-district map grid and a timeline (1912 → 1916 → 1917 → 1947 → 2000 bifurcation). Most Bihar GS questions are date–place–person triples; convert every fact above into that format and self-test.
    Examiner trap: confusing the first Buddhist council (Rajgir) with the third (Pataliputra), and Nalanda's founder-era (Gupta, 5th century CE) with its destroyer-era (12th–13th century). Keep the pairs apart: Rajgir = first, Pataliputra = third.

    12. Reasoning and Quantitative Aptitude for Teacher Recruitment

    Number sense: the non-negotiables

    • Divisibility shortcuts: by 3 — digit sum divisible by 3; by 4 — last two digits divisible by 4; by 11 — the difference of alternating digit sums is 0 or a multiple of 11. A century year is a leap year only if divisible by 400.
    • HCF and LCM: . Use this backwards: if the product and one of them are known, the other follows without listing factors.
    • BODMAS discipline: brackets, then orders (powers/roots), then division and multiplication left to right, then addition and subtraction. Most 'silly mistakes' are order-of-operations violations — write the order down before computing.
    • Parity rules: odd + odd = even, even + odd = odd, odd × odd = odd. Eliminate options before calculating: if the answer must be even, strike the odd options first.
    • Standard approximations: . Memorise the fraction–decimal pairs up to 1/12.

    Percentages, ratios and averages

    • Percentage change = (change ÷ original value) × 100 — the denominator is always the original, never the new value.
    • Successive changes: a 20% rise then a 20% fall gives a net 4% fall, not zero. Formula for x% up then y% down: net = x − y − xy/100.
    • Ratios: if A:B = 2:3 and B:C = 4:5, align B: multiply to get A:B:C = 8:12:15. Always express compound ratios with a common middle term.
    • Averages: average = sum ÷ count. When numbers are symmetric around a middle value, the average is the middle value — no addition needed.
    • Simple interest = P × R × T ÷ 100. Keep time in years and rate per annum consistent.

    Algebra and mensuration in one page

    • Identities: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b); (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²; (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b². 12² − 11² = 23 instantly, via (12−11)(12+11).
    • Sums: first n naturals = n(n+1)/2; first n odd numbers = n². Recognise triangular and square numbers on sight.
    • Geometry facts: angles of a triangle sum to 180°, of a quadrilateral 360°; angles round a point 360°; circumference 2πr, circle area πr²; triangle area ½ × base × height; cuboid volume = l × b × h.
    • Clock logic: the hands coincide 11 times every 12 hours, and the minute hand gains 5.5° per minute on the hour hand.
    • Unit conversion: 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s; 1 m/s = 18/5 km/h. Convert before comparing speeds.

    Reasoning: the high-frequency families

    • Series: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30 → next 42, following n(n+1). Check differences first, then differences of differences, then n²/n³ patterns.
    • Coding–decoding: map letters to positions (A = 1 … Z = 26) immediately; most codes are +k/−k shifts, reversals or position squares.
    • Blood relations: draw the family tree with generations before reading the options — never reason in your head alone.
    • Direction sense: at sunrise shadows point west. Draw the compass, mark the starting point, and track each turn as left/right of the current facing.
    • Statement–conclusion: a conclusion must follow strictly from the statements; 'some' never implies 'all', and middle terms cannot jump.
    • Odd one out: find the rule the majority follows, then name the breaker — the rule matters more than the answer.
    • Mirror vs water image: mirror swaps left–right; water image flips top–bottom.

    Exam temperament: scoring what you know

    • CTET has no negative marking — attempt every question. In exams with negative marking, your first pass answers only the sure ones; the second pass takes calculated risks.
    • Two-pass method: first pass — questions solvable under 45 seconds; mark the rest. Second pass — the marked ones with fresh eyes. Never let one question consume five minutes.
    • Option elimination first: in at least a third of aptitude questions, two options violate a basic constraint (parity, magnitude, units). Strike them before computing.
    • Reasonableness check: after computing, ask whether the answer's size makes sense — 20% of 450 cannot be 9,000. This single habit catches most arithmetic slips.
    • Practice as testing: solve mixed sets under a timer, then log every error by family (divisibility, ratio, series…). Your error log, reviewed weekly, is worth more than another hundred fresh questions.
    Examiner trap: successive percentage changes and 'average speed' questions punish formula-plugging without understanding. A car going 60 km/h one way and 40 km/h back does not average 50 km/h — it's 2xy/(x+y) = 48 km/h, because more time is spent at the slower speed.

    One-look revision board

    Use these as recall prompts. Cover the answer, say it aloud, then check.

    Pedagogy: the high-scoring distinctions

    • Growth is mainly quantitative; development includes qualitative change.
    • Readiness is not waiting passively; teaching and support can extend capability.
    • Equality gives the same resource; equity gives support needed for fair access.
    • Assessment of learning judges; for learning guides; as learning builds self-monitoring.
    • Intrinsic motivation comes from interest/mastery; extrinsic motivation comes from external reward or consequence.
    • Divergent questions allow several reasoned answers; convergent questions narrow to one.

    Think like the examiner

    When two answers look plausible, prefer the one that:

    Observesfinds the learner’s current idea
    Scaffoldssupports without doing the task
    Reflectsuses evidence to plan next steps

    Distractors often use absolutes—“always”, “only”, “all children”—or confuse silence and memorisation with learning.

    Rapid-fire one-liners — 300 facts

    One-sentence recall prompts across every chapter above. Use the search to drill a weak area.

    • Piaget: a schema is the mental model a child uses to interpret experience; new schemas form through adaptation.
    • Piaget: assimilation fits new experience into old schemas; accommodation reshapes the schema itself.
    • Piaget: equilibration is the drive to resolve disequilibrium, when new experience clashes with old schemas.
    • Piaget: object permanence emerges around 8–9 months — the infant knows things exist even when unseen.
    • Piaget: egocentrism — the pre-operational child cannot easily take another's viewpoint (the three-mountain task).
    • Piaget: animism — the pre-operational child attributes life and intention to inanimate objects.
    • Piaget: centration — focusing on one striking feature of a situation while ignoring the others.
    • Piaget: conservation (quantity stays the same despite appearance change) is mastered in the concrete operational stage.
    • Piaget: reversibility — mentally undoing an action — appears with concrete operations.
    • Piaget: class inclusion — understanding that a subclass belongs to a larger class — is a concrete-operational achievement.
    • Piaget: formal operational thought brings hypothetical-deductive (if–then) and propositional reasoning.
    • Piaget: moral development moves from heteronomous morality (rules fixed, punishment-focused) to autonomous morality.
    • Vygotsky: the More Knowledgeable Other (MKO) can be a teacher, a peer, or even a tool that advances learning.
    • Vygotsky: private speech (children talking aloud to guide themselves) gradually becomes silent inner speech.
    • Vygotsky: language is the primary psychological tool; thought and language merge around age two.
    • Vygotsky: culture supplies the tools — language, symbols, practices — through which the mind develops.
    • Bandura: the Bobo doll experiments (1961) showed children imitate observed aggression — learning without direct reward.
    • Bandura: observational learning needs four processes — attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation.
    • Bandura: self-efficacy — belief in one's capability — is built most strongly by mastery experiences.
    • Bandura: reciprocal determinism — person, behaviour, and environment continuously influence each other.
    • Pavlov: the UCS (food) triggers the UCR (salivation); after pairing, the CS (bell) alone triggers the CR.
    • Pavlov: extinction — the conditioned response fades when the CS repeatedly appears without the UCS.
    • Pavlov: generalization is responding to stimuli similar to the CS; discrimination is responding only to the exact CS.
    • Pavlov: spontaneous recovery — an extinguished response can briefly reappear after a rest period.
    • Thorndike: the law of effect — responses followed by satisfaction are stamped in; those followed by discomfort fade.
    • Thorndike: the law of readiness — learning works best when the learner is mentally set for the connection.
    • Thorndike: cats in puzzle boxes learned by trial and error — the basis of his S–R connectionism.
    • Skinner: positive reinforcement adds something pleasant; negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant — both strengthen behaviour.
    • Skinner: punishment suppresses behaviour but, unlike reinforcement, does not teach the desired alternative.
    • Skinner: a variable-ratio schedule (reward after an unpredictable number of responses) is most resistant to extinction.
    • Skinner: shaping builds complex behaviour through successive approximations — rewarding closer and closer steps.
    • Skinner: a token economy is classroom operant conditioning — tokens earned for desired behaviour, exchanged for rewards.
    • Gagné: his nine events of instruction run from gaining attention to enhancing retention and transfer.
    • Gagné: five learned capabilities — verbal information, intellectual skills, cognitive strategies, motor skills, attitudes.
    • Bruner: the spiral curriculum revisits key ideas at increasing depth as the learner matures.
    • Bruner: enactive (action) → iconic (image) → symbolic (language) is his sequence of representation.
    • Bruner: discovery learning — learners uncover principles themselves rather than receiving them stated.
    • Bruner (with Wood and Ross, 1976) gave us the term 'scaffolding' for temporary support inside the ZPD.
    • Ausubel: an advance organizer — a broad introductory framework — anchors new material to what the learner already knows.
    • Ausubel: meaningful learning connects new ideas to existing cognitive structure; rote learning stores them in isolation.
    • Ausubel: subsumption — new information is absorbed under broader, already-known concepts.
    • Erikson: trust vs. mistrust (infancy) — consistent care builds the hope that needs will be met.
    • Erikson: autonomy vs. shame and doubt (toddlerhood) — the virtue of will grows from guided choice.
    • Erikson: initiative vs. guilt (preschool) — purposeful play builds the virtue of purpose.
    • Erikson: industry vs. inferiority (school age) — mastering skills builds competence; failure breeds inferiority.
    • Erikson: identity vs. role confusion (adolescence) — the 'who am I?' crisis resolves into fidelity.
    • Erikson: intimacy vs. isolation (young adulthood), generativity vs. stagnation (middle age), integrity vs. despair (old age).
    • Freud: id (pleasure), ego (reality), superego (morality) — personality is their constant negotiation.
    • Freud: psychosexual stages — oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital — fixation at a stage shapes adult traits.
    • Kohlberg: Stage 1 (punishment–obedience) and Stage 2 (instrumental exchange) form the pre-conventional level.
    • Kohlberg: Stage 3 (good boy/nice girl) and Stage 4 (law and order) form the conventional level.
    • Kohlberg: Stage 5 (social contract) and Stage 6 (universal ethical principles) form the post-conventional level.
    • Kohlberg: the Heinz dilemma (steal a drug to save a life?) probes the reasoning behind a moral choice, not the choice itself.
    • Gilligan's critique: Kohlberg's stages undervalue an ethic of care — relationships and responsibility, not just justice.
    • Maslow: needs ascend from physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualization.
    • Maslow: lower (deficiency) needs must be reasonably met before growth needs motivate learning.
    • Rogers: unconditional positive regard, empathy, and congruence make the teacher a facilitator, not a director.
    • Rogers: significant learning is self-initiated and whole-person — it changes behaviour and attitudes, not just facts.
    • Dewey: 'learning by doing' — education is life itself, and the school a miniature democratic society.
    • Dewey: Democracy and Education (1916) argues the school must prepare citizens through shared experience.
    • Montessori: the prepared environment lets the child teach herself — auto-education through didactic materials.
    • Montessori: sensitive periods are windows when the child learns a skill (order, language, movement) with unusual ease.
    • Montessori: the absorbent mind (0–6 years) soaks up the environment without conscious effort.
    • Froebel: the kindergarten ('children's garden') — play is the child's serious work; gifts and occupations structure it.
    • Pestalozzi: education must address head, heart, and hands together — intellect, feeling, and craft.
    • Herbart: the five formal steps of a lesson — preparation, presentation, association, generalization, application.
    • Herbart: apperception — new ideas are understood only by linking them to the existing mass of ideas.
    • Rousseau: Emile argues for 'negative education' — shield the child from corrupting pressure and let nature lead.
    • Comenius: the 'father of modern education'; Didactica Magna proposed teaching 'everything to everybody'.
    • Locke: the mind as tabula rasa (blank slate) — experience writes knowledge upon it.
    • Tagore: Shantiniketan (1901) — learning in nature's lap, free from rigid classrooms; Visva-Bharati founded 1921.
    • Gandhi: Nai Talim (Basic education, Wardha 1937) — craft-centred learning uniting hand, head, and heart.
    • Aurobindo: integral education develops five aspects — physical, vital, mental, psychic, and spiritual.
    • Savitribai Phule: with Jyotiba Phule, opened India's first girls' school at Pune in 1848.
    • Gijubhai Badheka: brought Montessori ideas to India through Balmandir; wrote Divaswapna on child-centred teaching.
    • Tarabai Modak: pioneered the Balwadi (village preschool) movement from Kosbad, Maharashtra.
    • Krishnamurti: education must free the mind from fear — awareness, not conditioning, is its aim (Rishi Valley).
    • Vivekananda: education is the 'manifestation of the perfection already in man' — man-making, character-building.
    • Freire: Pedagogy of the Oppressed (1968) rejects the 'banking concept' — students as empty vessels to be filled.
    • Freire: problem-posing, dialogic education builds conscientization — critical awareness that transforms reality.
    • Bernstein: restricted code (context-bound everyday speech) vs. elaborated code (explicit, context-free) — schools reward the latter.
    • Bourdieu: cultural capital — the tastes, language, and credentials of the home — converts into school advantage.
    • Ebbinghaus: the forgetting curve — memory decays steeply at first; spaced review flattens the curve.
    • Tolman: rats formed cognitive maps of mazes — latent learning occurs without any reinforcement.
    • Köhler: Sultan the chimpanzee showed insight learning — sudden 'aha' restructuring, not trial and error.
    • Lewin: behaviour is a function of person and environment — B = f(P, E); the life space holds all influencing forces.
    • Lewin: coined 'action research' and 'group dynamics'; democratic leadership beats authoritarian and laissez-faire for morale.
    • Bronfenbrenner: development sits in nested systems — micro, meso, exo, macro, and the chronosystem of time.
    • Bowlby: attachment is an evolved bond; Ainsworth's Strange Situation revealed secure, avoidant, and ambivalent patterns.
    • Gesell: maturation governs development — norms unfold on a biological timetable; co-twin studies proved practice can't rush it.
    • Binet and Simon's 1905 scale was the first practical intelligence test — built to identify children needing help, not to rank all.
    • Terman's Stanford-Binet adapted Binet's test for America and introduced the IQ (mental age ÷ chronological age × 100).
    • Wechsler scales (WISC for children, WAIS for adults) measure verbal and performance IQ separately.
    • Spearman: the g factor — one general intelligence underlying all mental tasks — plus task-specific s factors.
    • Thurstone: seven primary mental abilities — intelligence is a profile, not a single number.
    • Cattell: fluid intelligence (novel reasoning) peaks young; crystallized intelligence (accumulated knowledge) grows with age.
    • Gardner: eight intelligences — linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalistic.
    • Gardner later proposed a ninth, existential intelligence — the capacity to ponder ultimate questions.
    • Sternberg: triarchic theory — analytical, creative, and practical intelligence together make 'successful intelligence'.
    • Emotional intelligence was formulated by Salovey and Mayer (1990) and popularized by Goleman (1995).
    • Goleman: five EI domains — self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills.
    • Guilford's Structure of Intellect crossed operations × contents × products — predicting 120+ distinct abilities.
    • Guilford: convergent thinking narrows to one right answer; divergent thinking branches into many.
    • Torrance: the TTCT measures fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration in creative thinking.
    • Creativity's threshold theory: beyond roughly IQ 120, more IQ adds little to creative output.
    • Deci and Ryan: self-determination theory — autonomy, competence, and relatedness fuel intrinsic motivation.
    • Weiner: attribution theory — learners explain outcomes by the locus, stability, and controllability of causes.
    • Weiner: attributing failure to controllable effort sustains motivation; blaming fixed ability kills it.
    • McClelland: three learned needs — achievement (nAch), power (nPow), affiliation (nAff).
    • Herzberg: hygiene factors (pay, conditions) prevent dissatisfaction; motivators (growth, recognition) create satisfaction.
    • Vroom: expectancy theory — motivation = expectancy × instrumentality × valence.
    • Locke and Latham: specific, challenging goals with feedback outperform vague 'do your best' goals.
    • Keller's ARCS model designs motivation in — Attention, Relevance, Confidence, Satisfaction.
    • Hull: drive-reduction theory — behaviour aims to reduce uncomfortable drives like hunger or anxiety.
    • Alderfer's ERG theory compresses Maslow into Existence, Relatedness, and Growth needs.
    • Intrinsic motivation outlasts extrinsic: rewards can even undermine interest (the overjustification effect).
    • Goal orientations: mastery goals (learn to improve) beat performance goals (look smart) for deep learning.
    • Self-regulated learning (Zimmerman): plan, monitor, and reflect — the learner steers her own learning cycle.
    • Flavell coined 'metacognition' — thinking about one's own thinking; it spans knowledge, experiences, and strategies.
    • Dweck: a growth mindset (ability can grow) invites challenge; a fixed mindset avoids it.
    • Information processing (Atkinson–Shiffrin): sensory register → short-term → long-term memory.
    • Miller: short-term memory holds about 7 ± 2 chunks — chunking expands what fits.
    • Baddeley's working memory: phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, central executive, episodic buffer.
    • Sweller's cognitive load theory: cut extraneous load, manage intrinsic load, build germane load.
    • Paivio's dual coding: words plus images are remembered better than either alone.
    • Retrieval practice (the testing effect — Roediger and Karpicke): recalling strengthens memory far more than re-reading.
    • Spaced practice beats massed practice (cramming) for durable learning.
    • Interleaving — mixing problem types — builds discrimination better than blocked drilling.
    • Elaboration: connecting new facts to what you know (self-explanation, examples) deepens encoding.
    • Kolb's experiential cycle: concrete experience → reflective observation → abstract conceptualization → active experimentation.
    • Marton and Säljö: deep learning seeks meaning; surface learning memorizes for the test.
    • Biggs: constructive alignment — objectives, teaching, and assessment must all point the same way.
    • Lave and Wenger: situated learning — knowledge lives in communities of practice, learned through legitimate peripheral participation.
    • Connectivism (Siemens and Downes): in a networked age, learning is forming connections across people and machines.
    • Knowles: andragogy — adults learn best when self-directed, experience-based, and problem-centred.
    • Heutagogy (Hase and Kenyon) goes further: the learner determines even what is learned — self-determined learning.
    • Ladson-Billings: culturally relevant pedagogy uses students' culture as a vehicle for learning.
    • Novak: concept maps make the structure of knowledge visible — nodes linked by labelled relationships.
    • Feuerstein: mediated learning experience — a mediator helps the learner go beyond direct exposure; the root of dynamic assessment.
    • De Bono: lateral thinking breaks set patterns; the Six Thinking Hats separate modes of thought.
    • Differentiation (Tomlinson): vary content, process, product, or environment to meet diverse readiness levels.
    • UDL (CAST): design for all from the start — multiple means of engagement, representation, and action/expression.
    • Wait time (Rowe): pausing 3+ seconds after a question raises the quality and length of student answers.
    • Think-Pair-Share (Lyman): think alone, discuss with a partner, then share — every voice gets rehearsal.
    • Jigsaw (Aronson): each student masters one piece, then teaches it — cooperation becomes necessary, not optional.
    • Reciprocal teaching (Palincsar and Brown): students take turns predicting, questioning, clarifying, summarizing.
    • KWL (Ogle): chart what you Know, Want to know, and Learned — a reading-thinking frame.
    • Numbered Heads Together (Kagan): groups confer, then a randomly called number answers — individual accountability built in.
    • STAD (Slavin): team study followed by individual quizzes; team scores reward improvement, not just top marks.
    • Group Investigation (Sharan): students plan, carry out, and present their own inquiry — high student ownership.
    • The 5E model (Bybee): Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate — inquiry in five moves.
    • Polya's four steps of problem solving: understand the problem, devise a plan, carry out the plan, look back.
    • Dienes: six stages of math learning — free play, games, searching for commonalities, representation, symbolization, formalization.
    • van Hiele levels of geometric thinking: visualization → analysis → abstraction → deduction → rigor.
    • Skemp: instrumental understanding (rules without reasons) vs. relational understanding (knowing why).
    • CPA sequence (Bruner): concrete manipulatives → pictorial diagrams → abstract symbols.
    • Socratic questioning probes assumptions, evidence, and implications rather than fishing for one answer.
    • A hinge question is a diagnostic checkpoint — the lesson turns on whether students answer it correctly.
    • Exit tickets: a 2-minute end-of-lesson probe that tells the teacher what stuck and what didn't.
    • Microteaching (Allen and Ryan, Stanford): teach a 5–10 minute mini-lesson, get feedback, re-teach — skills built in cycles.
    • Scriven (1967) coined formative and summative evaluation — the terms assessors still use.
    • Bloom's mastery learning: with feedback and corrective time, most students can reach mastery — aptitude is time needed.
    • Glaser: criterion-referenced tests judge against fixed standards; norm-referenced tests rank against peers.
    • Ipsative assessment compares a learner with her own past performance — growth, not rank.
    • Authentic assessment (Wiggins): real-world tasks — performances and products — not just paper tests.
    • Dynamic assessment measures learning potential during mediated support, not just current unaided performance.
    • Analytic rubrics score separate criteria; holistic rubrics give one overall judgement.
    • Reliability types: test–retest (stability), parallel forms (equivalence), split-half and Cronbach's alpha (internal consistency), inter-rater.
    • Validity types: content (coverage), criterion — concurrent and predictive — and construct (does it measure the trait?).
    • Black and Wiliam's 'Inside the Black Box' (1998) showed assessment for learning can raise achievement substantially.
    • NEP 2020 (approved 29 July 2020) replaced the National Policy on Education, 1986 (modified 1992).
    • The Kasturirangan Committee's draft (2019) became the blueprint of NEP 2020.
    • NEP 2020's 5+3+3+4 design: Foundational (ages 3–8), Preparatory (8–11), Middle (11–14), Secondary (14–18).
    • NEP target: 100% Gross Enrolment Ratio from preschool to secondary by 2030; 50% in higher education by 2035.
    • NEP: the medium of instruction till at least Grade 5 — preferably till Grade 8 — should be the home/local language.
    • NEP ends hard stream separation — a student can mix science with music, arts with vocational skills.
    • NEP: coding and vocational exposure begin at the middle stage (from class 6), with bagless internship days.
    • The 4-year integrated B.Ed. becomes the minimum teaching qualification by 2030.
    • MHRD was renamed the Ministry of Education under NEP 2020.
    • NEP proposes HECI — one umbrella regulator with four verticals — to subsume the roles of UGC, AICTE, and NCTE.

    • NIPUN Bharat: the national mission for foundational literacy and numeracy by the end of Grade 3 (target 2026–27).

    CTET · Pedagogy

    A four-week revision route

    Designed for a working aspirant: two 45-minute blocks on weekdays, one mock-and-review block on the weekend.

    WEEK 01

    Build the base

    • Development principles + Piaget/Vygotsky
    • Language acquisition and comprehension
    • Number sense / Bihar anchor facts
    • Weekend: 50-question baseline
    WEEK 02

    Teach each subject

    • Math misconceptions and manipulatives
    • EVS inquiry and themes
    • Science or Social Science pedagogy
    • Weekend: review every wrong answer
    WEEK 03

    Mix and retrieve

    • Alternate content and pedagogy sets
    • Language accuracy drills
    • TRE GS arithmetic and reasoning
    • Weekend: timed full paper
    WEEK 04

    Close the gaps

    • Revise error notebook, not everything
    • Two timed section tests
    • Memorise formulas and distinctions
    • Last day: light recall and rest
